prompt: Why does the course keep every Postman collection as a JSON file in your project?
hint: Whose terms decide what the free plan keeps?

choices.text: Postman cannot open a collection unless it comes from a file
choices.why: Postman keeps collections in its own cloud workspace without any file of yours.

choices.text: A file stays yours whatever Postman's plan becomes
choices.why: Right. Newman runs it without an account, and git keeps its history.

choices.text: JSON files make the requests faster
choices.why: The request on the wire is the same text whichever way it was stored.

choices.text: boxoffice only answers requests that come from a saved file
choices.why: boxoffice cannot tell which program asked, let alone where the request was stored.

prompt: You run boxoffice inside WSL on Windows. Which Postman do you install, and what address does it use?
hint: What does WSL do with localhost?

choices.text: The Linux version, inside WSL, at localhost:8080
choices.why: Postman needs a graphical desktop, which the Windows side has.

choices.text: The Windows version, at the WSL machine's own IP address
choices.why: No address to look up: WSL passes localhost through to Windows.

choices.text: The Windows version, at localhost:8080
choices.why: Right. WSL passes localhost through, so nothing needs configuring.

choices.text: Neither: Postman cannot reach a server running in WSL
choices.why: It can, through the localhost WSL shares with Windows.

prompt: A colleague says boxoffice behaves differently when the request comes from Postman instead of curl. What does the lesson say about that?
hint: What travels on the wire?

choices.text: It is expected, because Postman is a test framework and curl is not
choices.why: Being able to run tests does not change what a request is.

choices.text: The server sees the same kind of text either way, so look for a difference in what was sent
choices.why: Right. Section 03 says where to look: the headers Postman adds.

choices.text: Postman talks to the API through its own cloud first
choices.why: A request to localhost goes straight from your computer to boxoffice.

choices.text: boxoffice reads the program's name and answers it differently
choices.why: boxoffice reads no User-Agent at all; read its source.

prompt: A test checks that a response body has its fields in a particular order. Which body view should you read?
hint: Which view shows the bytes as they arrived?

choices.text: Pretty, because it shows one field per line
choices.why: Pretty parses and lays the body out again, so it shows Postman's arrangement, not the server's.

choices.text: Raw
choices.why: Right. Raw is the text as it arrived, untouched.

choices.text: Preview
choices.why: Preview renders the body as a page would; it is for HTML.

choices.text: The Headers tab, where the order is listed
choices.why: Headers lists the response headers, not the fields of the body.

prompt: A request answers 200 in Postman and 400 from your app, with the same address, method and body. Where does the section tell you to look first?
hint: Postman sends more than you typed.

choices.text: At the time pane, since a slow app is refused
choices.why: A 400 says the request was wrong, not slow.

choices.text: At boxoffice's source, since the server must be choosing at random
choices.why: The same request gets the same answer; the requests differ.

choices.text: At the size pane, which shows the request's headers
choices.why: The size is of the response, headers and body together.

choices.text: At the extra headers Postman added, shown in its Console
choices.why: Right. A header Postman sends and your app does not is a likely difference.

prompt: Match what Postman shows to what lesson 1 called it.
hint: The table in the section.

prompt: showId is sh-103 in the collection and sh-102 in the active environment. You edited the collection a minute ago. Which value is sent?
hint: Time does not decide it.

choices.text: sh-103, because it was set most recently
choices.why: Which was set last does not matter; the scope does.

choices.text: sh-102, because the environment is narrower
choices.why: Right. Precedence goes by scope, and the environment is narrower than the collection.

choices.text: Neither: Postman refuses a name defined twice
choices.why: Defining a name in two scopes is normal and is how an environment overrides a default.

choices.text: Both, one after the other
choices.why: A variable resolves to one value per request.

prompt: Put Postman's variable scopes in order from the widest to the narrowest.
hint: The last one lives for one request.

prompt: The collection defines token with a valid value, and the active environment has a token variable left empty. What does an order request send?
hint: Does an empty value count as defined?

choices.text: The collection's token, because an empty value is skipped
choices.why: An empty value is a value; Postman does not skip it.

choices.text: The literal text {{token}}, because the name is unresolved
choices.why: The name is resolved: the environment defines it, as empty.

choices.text: An empty token, and a 401
choices.why: Right. The environment is narrower, and its empty value wins.

choices.text: Postman stops and asks which of the two to use
choices.why: Precedence decides without asking.

prompt: Postman replaces a name written in double braces, such as `{{baseUrl}}`, with its value ___ the request is sent.
hint: The server never sees the braces.

prompt: clientSecret has the type secret in the lab environment. What does that protect?
hint: Look at the env transcript.

choices.text: What the screen shows
choices.why: Right. The file on disk still holds ci-secret in plain text.

choices.text: The file, which Postman encrypts on export
choices.why: jq printed ci-secret straight out of the file.

choices.text: The request, which sends the secret encrypted
choices.why: The type changes how Postman draws the value, not what is sent.

choices.text: Nothing at all; it is a label for people
choices.why: It does something: it hides the value on screen.

prompt: The copy of the environment with a missing comma made jq stop. On which line did jq report the error?
hint: Read the broken transcript.

prompt: Your team shares the lab environment file through git. Where should the real secret of a real API go?
hint: Postman keeps two values per variable.

choices.text: In the file, with the type set to secret
choices.why: secret only hides the value on screen; the file still carries it to everyone.

choices.text: In a collection variable instead, which is not exported
choices.why: A collection variable travels inside the collection file.

choices.text: Typed into Postman on your machine only
choices.why: Right. The value that stays on your computer is not exported.

choices.text: In the address, as a query parameter
choices.why: An address ends up in logs; lesson 3 said why credentials go in a header.

prompt: In which order does a run of the whole collection send its requests?
hint: The names transcript.

choices.text: Alphabetical order of the request names
choices.why: Get token would then come before List shows; it does not.

choices.text: In the order the requests were last edited
choices.why: Editing changes nothing about the order.

choices.text: Top to bottom, as the file lists them
choices.why: Right. That is why a request can use what an earlier one received.

choices.text: All at once, in parallel
choices.why: They run one after the other; nothing could be chained otherwise.

prompt: Why does the shows folder set noauth instead of inheriting the collection's bearer token?
hint: What would a token hide?

choices.text: boxoffice refuses any request to /v1/shows that carries a token
choices.why: boxoffice ignores the header there; that is not the reason.

choices.text: So a show list that wrongly demanded a token would fail
choices.why: Right. Sending a token where none is needed hides that defect.

choices.text: Folders cannot inherit from a collection
choices.why: orders inherits, which the auth transcript shows.

choices.text: A token on a GET makes the request slower to send
choices.why: One header changes nothing measurable here.

prompt: Which of these send an Authorization header with the bearer token, in the lesson's collection?
hint: Follow the inheritance from request to folder to collection.

choices.text: Create order
choices.why: Right: orders inherits the collection's bearer.

choices.text: Get token
choices.why: Its folder, auth, sets noauth.

choices.text: Cancel order
choices.why: Right: same folder, same inheritance.

choices.text: One show
choices.why: The shows folder sets noauth.

choices.text: Read order
choices.why: Right: it inherits through orders.

prompt: According to the used transcript, how many times does the collection use {{baseUrl}}?
hint: uniq -c counts.

prompt: You run the collection by hand a second time without restarting boxoffice. Create order answers 201 and Read order answers 200, but for an order that was cancelled earlier. What happened?
hint: Where does orderId come from?

choices.text: Create order failed silently and returned the old order
choices.why: It answered 201 with a new order; boxoffice numbered it ord-1002.

choices.text: Read order still asks for ord-1001, the first run's order
choices.why: Right. orderId is fixed, while the new order is ord-1002; lesson 5 saves location instead.

choices.text: Postman cached the first answer to Read order
choices.why: Even with a cache, the request itself asked for ord-1001.

choices.text: The token from the first run had expired
choices.why: An expired token answers 401, not 200.

prompt: The same collection must run against a staging server at a different address with its own client. What do you change?
hint: What is an environment for?

choices.text: Every request's address, from localhost to the staging host
choices.why: That is the twenty edits {{baseUrl}} exists to avoid.

choices.text: The collection's variables, then change them back afterwards
choices.why: baseUrl and the credentials are not collection variables here, and editing back and forth is how a run goes to the wrong server.

choices.text: A global variable, so every collection sees the new address
choices.why: Globals are the widest scope; the environment would hide it anyway.

choices.text: Nothing in the collection: a staging environment with its own values
choices.why: Right. Switching environments points the same requests elsewhere.

prompt: After lunch every order request in your Postman answers 401 with error_description="token expired", while the shows still answer 200. What explains both?
hint: Which requests carry the token at all?

choices.text: The token expired; the shows send none
choices.why: Right. Ask for a new token and paste it again; lesson 5 automates that.

choices.text: boxoffice restarted and forgot every token it issued
choices.why: boxoffice keeps no list of tokens; a restart would not make it say expired.

choices.text: The lab environment was switched off
choices.why: With no environment, baseUrl would not resolve and nothing would answer at all.

choices.text: The collection's bearer setting changed to noauth
choices.why: Then the answer would be no bearer token, not token expired.

prompt: A new request in the orders folder sends the body {"show_id": "sh-101", "seats": {{seatCount}}}, and no scope defines seatCount. What happens when Postman sends it?
hint: An undefined name is not replaced.

choices.text: Postman sends 0 in its place
choices.why: Postman has no default value for an unknown name.

choices.text: Postman asks for the value before sending
choices.why: It draws the name in red and sends anyway if you press Send.

choices.text: The braces go out as text, and boxoffice answers 400 for a body that is not JSON
choices.why: Right. {{seatCount}} unquoted in the body makes it invalid JSON.

choices.text: The global scope supplies the value
choices.why: Only if somebody defined it there; nobody did.
